question: Which statement best describes Dynamic import()?
options: React.lazy reads module.default and assumes it is a component. To lazy-load a named export you must remap it to default inside the import promise. This trips people up because the import succeeds but renders nothing useful when the default is missing.

React.lazy(() => import('./C')) wraps a dynamic import into a component React can render. While the chunk downloads the component suspends; once the promise resolves React renders it, and the chunk is cached so future renders are instant. It expects the module to resolve to an object with a default export that is a component — named exports must be remapped.

A runtime, promise-returning form of import that signals the bundler to emit the target module as a separate chunk loaded on demand, rather than baking it into the main bundle. When execution reaches the import(), the browser fetches that .js chunk over the network and resolves a promise with the module. It is the foundation every code-splitting tool builds on.

A lazy component must be rendered inside a <Suspense> boundary that provides a fallback, because while its chunk downloads it suspends by throwing a promise. The nearest Suspense ancestor catches that signal and shows the fallback during the fetch. With no boundary above it, React has nowhere to show the loading state and throws an error — a very common beginner mistake.

question: Which statement best describes React.lazy?
options: Route-based splitting makes each page its own chunk — the highest-leverage, lowest-effort split and the right default, since users download only the page they navigate to. Component-based splitting defers an individual heavy or rarely-used widget (an editor, chart, map, or modal) within a page. Use routes as the baseline, then add component-level splits for specific bloated widgets.

question: Which statement best describes Suspense pairing?
options: Route-based splitting makes each page its own chunk — the highest-leverage, lowest-effort split and the right default, since users download only the page they navigate to. Component-based splitting defers an individual heavy or rarely-used widget (an editor, chart, map, or modal) within a page. Use routes as the baseline, then add component-level splits for specific bloated widgets.

Splitting trades a smaller initial bundle for extra network requests on navigation, which can feel slow. Prefetching hides that latency by warming a chunk before the user needs it — calling its import() on link hover, during idle time, or via bundler magic comments like webpackPrefetch. The chunk lands in cache so navigation feels instant without bloating the initial load.

question: Which statement best describes Default export requirement and named exports?
options: Route-based splitting makes each page its own chunk — the highest-leverage, lowest-effort split and the right default, since users download only the page they navigate to. Component-based splitting defers an individual heavy or rarely-used widget (an editor, chart, map, or modal) within a page. Splitting trades a smaller initial bundle for extra network requests on navigation, which can feel slow. Prefetching hides that latency by warming a chunk before the user needs it — calling its import() on link hover, during idle time, or via bundler magic comments like webpackPrefetch. The chunk lands in cache so navigation feels instant without bloating the initial load.

Dynamic imports fail two ways: transient network errors, and stale references after a deploy when old hashed filenames no longer exist on the server. A rejected import() is an error, NOT a pending state, so Suspense cannot handle it — you must wrap lazy routes in an Error Boundary. Retry the import a few times with backoff for transient failures, and trigger a full page reload for the stale-deploy case so the client fetches the fresh manifest.

Splitting is not free at the extreme: too many tiny chunks add per-request overhead and can create loading waterfalls where one chunk must resolve before the next is even requested. The fix is to group related code into sensibly-sized chunks and prefetch likely-next ones, balancing initial bundle size against the number of round-trips.
